idiom_name: protected non-virtual provided operations plus a protected virtual sandbox method
implementation_notes: C++ is the language the chapter's own sample is written in: protected members are reachable from derived classes yet invisible to clients, and one protected pure virtual sandbox method forces every behaviour to implement it. Keep the provided operations non-virtual (the base keeps control of the vocabulary and can change its implementation without disturbing the family) and mark the entry point - and any primitive a subclass legitimately specialises - virtual, with override since C++11 so a signature drift becomes a compile error. The classic form needs no library or idiom beyond access specifiers and virtual dispatch; the CRTP variant is worth it only when the concrete behaviour types are known at compile time and the virtual call must disappear.
pitfalls: Protected virtual primitives are an invitation: once a primitive is virtual a subclass can replace the implementation for its whole subtree, so keep the primitives non-virtual unless specialisation is genuinely wanted.
Calling the sandbox method from the base constructor or destructor dispatches only as far as the class being built or torn down, so the behaviour's override is silently skipped.

A derived class declaring a member with the same name as a primitive hides the base member instead of overriding it; mark real overrides with override and give primitives names that cannot be stumbled into.
The destructor is part of the contract: make it public and virtual when deletion through Superpower* is allowed, otherwise protected and non-virtual, or undefined behaviour follows.

variants.name: CRTP mixin: compile-time sandbox with static dispatch
variants.idiom_name: template <class Derived> Sandbox mixin calling static_cast<Derived*>(this)->activate()
variants.implementation_notes: The same role split with no vtable: a class template parameterised by the derived type provides the primitives and calls the behaviour's activate() through static_cast (the curiously recurring template pattern), so every primitive call is monomorphised and inlinable. Choose it when the behaviour types are known at compile time and the virtual call is measurable in a hot loop - the standard library uses the same mechanism in enable_shared_from_this. The trade-off against the protected-primitives variant is type identity: Sandbox<A> and Sandbox<B> are unrelated types that cannot share a container or cross a virtual boundary without adding one, each instantiation emits its own copy of the primitives, and errors surface only when the template is instantiated.
pitfalls: CRTP instantiations are unrelated types: Sandbox<SkyLaunch> and Sandbox<FreezeRay> cannot sit in one container or be passed through a common virtual interface without introducing one.
The derived type is incomplete while the base is being constructed, so primitives and the entry point must not be called from the base constructor.
A behaviour that forgets to declare the base as a friend, or a typo in the derived type argument, surfaces as a template error at the instantiation site rather than at the definition.
